title: When Leaders Shouldnt Be Vulnerable
author: Admired Leadership
summary: While affirming that vulnerability builds trust and deepens relationships, this article argues that leaders should withhold disclosure on four specific topics. It cautions against sharing who they distrust or think poorly of within the organization, since such disclosures taint reputations and perceptions permanently. It also warns leaders against volunteering their own acts of kindness or self-assessed personal growth, both of which read as self-serving rather than authentic. Finally, it flags personal finances as an off-limits topic because disclosure creates status comparisons that widen distance rather than closing it. The piece closes by quoting Brene Brown on vulnerability as the birthplace of connection, while insisting that skilled leaders know where the line sits.
points: Leaders should never share who they distrust or view as unskilled, since it can permanently stain how peers see that person.
Volunteering your own good deeds or self-assessed progress reads as self-serving and undermines long-term credibility.
Personal finances and compensation are off-limits topics because they create status comparisons that widen distance rather than build connection.
Vulnerability shared too early in a professional relationship can create awkwardness rather than trust; timing matters as much as content.
quotes: Inclusive leaders view vulnerability as a leadership strength and not a weakness.
First on the list for leaders to keep to themselves is who they disrespect or think poorly of in the organization or on the team.
Second, good leaders should never share the acts of kindness and good deeds they do for others.
Personal wealth, compensation, and other financial information are off-limits because they create a social comparison that increases status and makes others feel less important.
Author Brené Brown suggests, “Vulnerability is the birthplace of connection and the path to feelings of worthiness.
